opening_message:
Ticket 1: Morgan Swanson (employee ID E037) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E037.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Morgan Swanson (E037) is a full_time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin requires owning role (Payroll Specialist), so write is the maximum. Requested write is at the maximum, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E037 is a contractor with basic security training (HR note said full_time; Security DB is authoritative for employment/training). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Basic training => max is read. Requested write is above max, so recommend read.
reason: E037 (Morgan Swanson) requested write access to Payroll. The Security agent's note indicates the Security DB (authoritative for employment type and training) shows E037 is a contractor with basic security training, despite HR listing full_time. Per policy, contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training. With basic training, the maximum is read, and the requested write is above the maximum. Grant the maximum: read.

content.text:
Let me carefully analyze this ticket.

The employee Morgan Swanson (E037) requests write access to Payroll.

There are conflicting notes:
- HR agent says: role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation write.
- Security agent says: role Engineer (not verified), employment type contractor (verified in Security DB), security training basic, recommendation read. Security agent says Security DB is authoritative for employment/training.

So the facts:
- Role: Engineer (both agree)
- Employment type: HR says full_time; Security says contractor. Security DB is authoritative.
- Security training: basic.

Policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If contractor with basic training: max = read. Requested write is above max, so grant read.

If full-time: max = write (role Engineer doesn't own Payroll; owner is Payroll Specialist). Requested write = max, grant write.

The question is which employment type to trust. The Security agent says Security DB is authoritative for employment/training. Hmm. The HR agent says they looked up in own database. The security agent looked up employment type in their own DB and says it's authoritative.

The team memory notes indicate: "Employee facts written on an earlier ticket are shown on later tickets about the same employee." This is ticket 1, so both notes are from the same ticket.

The decision depends on which source we trust. The security agent explicitly states their DB is authoritative for employment/training. Typically in such scenarios, the Security agent's DB is authoritative. So employment type = contractor, training = basic.

So max access = read. Requested write > read, so grant read.

Let me submit decision: read.

Reason: E037's Security DB record (authoritative for employment/training) shows contractor with basic security training. Contractors with basic training max at read; requested write exceeds max, so grant read.
